<reason>A (CON) built a clever case — net-worth accounting, default-as-ceiling, concession-stacking, appropriating the employer match as the tax code's own output — and argued it with real rhetorical force. But B (PRO) won the structural battle. B's pressure question demanding the mechanism by which any deduction gets a non-participant to his first dollar forced A's decisive concession in A4.1 ("no deduction nudges him directly"). A's escape — both policies miss the no-plan worker, so judge "everyone else" — was blunted by B's unrebutted employer-mandate point from B1.6 and by B contesting A's chosen ground: on moving savers from four to eight, B turned A's own inertia premise against him ("he has argued my mechanism into the winning position for his own scenario"), since price incentives require decisions the inattentive won't make while escalation harnesses the inertia A called permanent. A's net-worth counterfactual was real but never fully survived B's partial-offset, match, and "frictions need not disappear to leave a remainder above zero" answers; the ceiling argument lost to mass-at-zero; the match appropriation was neutralized by "exists in both worlds." B's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a small execution cost, but all substance (A1, A2, match, weighing) survived before the cut. A's closing spin that B "surrendered" the match misdescribed an exchange B actually won.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive chain: B's Q1 (name the mechanism for the non-participant's first dollar) → A4.1's admission that no deduction nudges him directly → B5.1–B5.2 converting that concession into the winning frame, using CON's own inertia premise to claim even the "everyone else" ground. Runner-up: B2.4's "a refundable credit is not a deduction; when CON reaches for it, he is fleeing the motion," which shrank A's design-flexibility route.</best_rebuttal>
